headline: Global summit charts path to protect children amid crises
meta_description: Over 600 delegates from 100+ countries gather in Uzbekistan to tackle threats to child wellbeing, from conflict to climate change, with concrete solutions.
summary_short: A UN-backed summit in Samarkand brings together world leaders to ensure children can thrive despite war, poverty, and climate chaos.
body:
More than 600 participants from over 100 countries converged in Samarkand, Uzbekistan this week for the World Summit Investing in Children's Wellbeing—a gathering driven by urgent mathematics and harder truths. UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that progress on child wellbeing faces existential threats from conflicts, economic pressures, health emergencies, and climate shocks. Yet his message carried a counterweight: "when we invest in children, we invest in the future." The summit's scope extends beyond single programmes to systemic change, recognising that a child's thriving depends on the interconnected availability of health, education, protection from violence, family support, and access to help when needed.

Uzbekistan's First Lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva delivered a sobering statistic: deaths among children under five are expected to rise in 2025 for the first time this century, amid a sharp decline in international humanitarian assistance. One billion children grow up in countries most vulnerable to climate change. Yet the host nation itself offers grounds for measured hope. Preschool enrolment in Uzbekistan has surged from 27 per cent in 2017 to 78 per cent in 2026. More than 10,000 children with disabilities now attend mainstream schools, and 1.5 million families receive social assistance.

The summit also spotlighted childhood cancer as a barometer of global inequality. While over 80 per cent of children with cancer are cured in high-income countries, the figure drops below 30 per cent in many low and middle-income countries. In Tashkent, an institution called Mehrli Maktab—meaning "caring school" in Uzbek—allows children aged two to 18 to continue their education during lengthy cancer treatment, studying everything from mathematics to music. The World Health Organization aims to increase global childhood cancer survival to 60 per cent by 2030, but only if investment and political commitment match the ambition.
quick_facts: 600+ delegates from 100+ countries attended Samarkand summit
Preschool enrolment in Uzbekistan rose from 27% to 78% since 2017
80%+ cure rate for child cancer in wealthy nations vs. under 30% in low-income countries
One billion children live in climate-vulnerable countries
Mehrli Maktab school in Tashkent serves children during cancer treatment
